The papers don't directly address lithium-free cathodes for lithium batteries. Every lithium-ion cathode they discuss (LiNiO2, NFA, NCA, NMC, LCO, LFP, V2O5, DRX) contains lithium by design. The "cobalt-free" and "zero-cobalt" cathodes in the 2020 and 2022 reviews still contain lithium.

The papers do describe lithium-free cathode chemistries, but in sodium systems:

- **Sodium-sulfur cathode (Carter et al., Nano Lett. 2017):** A sulfur cathode confined in sugar-derived microporous carbon, paired with a sodium anode in a glyme electrolyte, delivers over 700 mAh/gS at 0.1C, about 370 mAh/gS at 1C, and over 300 mAh/gS across 1500 cycles at 1C, with Coulombic efficiency above 98% (p. 1). The authors estimate an energy density of about 180 Wh/kg for the whole electrode mass (p. 5).

- **Presodiated pyrite cathode in an anode-free sodium cell (Cohn et al., Nano Lett. 2017):** Sodium metal is plated in situ on a carbon-coated Al current collector, and the pyrite (FeS2) cathode is presodiated before assembly. The full cell reaches about 400 Wh/kg based on the active mass of both electrodes (p. 4). The sodium is carried by the cathode, so this is lithium-free but not sodium-free.

- **Na3V2(PO4)3 cathode (cited in Bai et al., Materials Today 2020):** A fully recyclable bipolar sodium-ion battery using Na3V2(PO4)3 as cathode and Al as current collector was reported by Liu et al. (p. 9). This is described only as a cited example.

- **Other ions (Muralidharan et al., ACS Nano 2017):** The authors suggest strain engineering could extend to Na+, K+, Mg2+ and Ca2+ hosts, because strain might offset insertion barriers for larger ions (p. 6). This is a proposed direction, not a demonstrated result.

Caveats:
- Sodium is much heavier and larger than lithium, and the papers note its lower energy density (Cohn et al., p. 1) and the roughly 260% volume expansion of sodium versus about 80% for lithium in sulfur systems (Carter et al., p. 2).
- The Na-S and anode-free Na papers report performance from lab-scale coin and pouch-type cells. The Na-S paper is a proof of concept, and the pyrite paper says cathode optimization is still needed for better cycling and rate capability (Cohn et al., p. 4).
- None of the papers provides a lithium-free cathode for lithium batteries, so a lithium-ion battery would still need lithium in the cathode.

If you meant a battery with no lithium at all, the sodium-based work above is the closest match in these papers. If you meant a cathode that works with a lithium-free anode, the papers don't cover that case.
